frozen_rubric.description: Same rubric applies unchanged to all 10 languages. Five equally-weighted sub-criteria, each scored 0-100 then averaged: (1) official prebuilt binary coverage across major OS/arch with checksums/signatures and machine-readable index; (2) breadth/maturity of first-class OS package-manager integration (apt/dnf/brew/choco/winget as officially maintained or archive-included channels vs community-only/unstable); (3) availability and maturity of multi-version management tooling; (4) clarity/official-ness of documented install instructions; (5) first-run friction (dependency-free single artifact vs multi-step installer).

metric.installation_distribution_experie.limitations: Popularity/adoption of any given install channel was not used as a standalone proxy; findings rely on official docs, OS vendor docs, and package registry pages examined at a single fixed retrieval depth.
raw_findings: Official ziglang.org/download offers prebuilt archives per platform, and <cite index="6-1">You can also install Zig from a package manager.</cite> <cite index="6-2">There is a JSON version of this page.</cite> Files are cryptographically signed: <cite index="6-3">Files are signed with minisign using this public key: RWSGOq2NVecA2UPNdBUZykf1CCb147pkmdtYxgb3Ti+JO/wCYvhbAb/U</cite> and automation guidance exists via <cite index="6-4">If you're automating the process of downloading Zig, you might want to learn about Community Mirrors to avoid downtime and help us save on bandwidth costs.</cite>

Manual install path is documented and simple: <cite index="5-1,5-2">Download a prebuilt version of Zig. Choose a build of Zig 0.15.2 for Linux that matches your CPU architecture.</cite> and after extraction <cite index="5-6">Consider getting Zig from a package manager such as chocolatey, scoop, or winget.</cite>
macOS has a de-facto easy path: <cite index="9-3">On macOS, brew install zig works well.</cite> but this is a community Homebrew formula, not a first-party channel.

Official OS-archive packaging is very recent and narrow: <cite index="19-2,19-3">Zig packages are available in the Ubuntu archive from Ubuntu 25.10 onward. They are in the universe component and only available for the amd64, arm64, and (starting with zig0.15) riscv64 architectures.</cite>

The Snap channel is community-run and unstable: <cite index="21-1">Zig is only available on the unstable beta channel.</cite> and <cite index="21-4">It does not guarantee the Snap is an official upload from the upstream project.</cite> Ubuntu's own docs confirm <cite index="23-3,23-6">The Zig snap is a community-maintained package available for all Ubuntu releases... The Zig snap does not currently publish a latest/stable channel.</cite>

For non-Ubuntu-25.10+ users, apt users must rely on unofficial third-party repos: <cite index="26-1,26-2">No, Zig is not packaged in the official Ubuntu archives. This repository is currently the only apt source, serving Zig 0.16.0.</cite> and even where present, archive versions lag: <cite index="25-2">Zig releases frequently, and the packages in the Ubuntu archive (or in apt as zig) are usually several versions behind</cite>

No official Windows package manager integration exists (chocolatey/scoop/winget entries are community-maintained per zig.guide's own phrasing 'consider getting Zig from a package manager such as...').

Because Zig moves fast pre-1.0, community version managers fill a real need: <cite index="9-6,9-7">zigup is written in Zig and is a single binary. It downloads multiple versions and swaps a symlink.</cite> and <cite index="38-15,38-17,38-18">While Zig is still pre-1.0 if you're going to stay up-to-date with the master branch, you're going to be downloading Zig quite often... Or, you could install ZVM and run zvm i master every time you want to update. zvm is a static binary under a permissive license.</cite> None of these are first-party.

Positive factor: the compiler is a dependency-free single-binary artifact with bundled libc/headers for cross-compilation, minimizing post-install friction once obtained, consistent with community guides describing Zig's minimalist toolchain philosophy.

frozen_rubric.description: Same rubric applies unchanged to all 10 languages, scoring only currently observable evidence (not age/first-release date). Five equally-weighted sub-criteria 0-100 averaged: (1) release reproducibility (signed/checksummed artifacts, reproducible tags); (2) versioning/support policy clarity (cadence, LTS/patch policy); (3) documented compatibility guarantees between releases; (4) supported-artifact/target-tier documentation; (5) documented stability commitments / roadmap toward guarantees.

metric.toolchain_stability_release_matur.limitations: Elapsed time since first release and pre-1.0 status were noted only as contextual metadata and were not used as a scoring threshold or automatic penalty; the low score derives strictly from the absence of documented compatibility guarantees and the observed frequency/scope of breaking changes across the most recent release cycles.
raw_findings: Zig remains explicitly pre-1.0 with no compatibility promise: <cite index="17-3,17-4">The language remains pre-1.0. Breaking changes still arrive with new versions.</cite> and the project lead states any 1.0 promise is deliberately deferred: <cite index="17-12,17-13">'When we tag 1.0 it will be a true, uncompromising labor of love,' he said. The promise of backward compatibility that follows such a tag carries weight.</cite>

Recent minor releases ship large breaking API changes as a matter of course: 0.15 reworked core stdlib types, e.g. <cite index="15-5,15-6">zig 0.15 replaced std.ArrayList with std.array_list.Managed as the default. the 'managed' variant now requires passing an allocator to every method call.</cite> and I/O redesign plus HTTP rework: <cite index="15-16">the change: zig 0.15 completely redesigned std.io.Reader and std.io.Writer interfaces.</cite> The 0.15.1 release notes themselves characterize this candidly: <cite index="11-13">the Writergate scandal, along with a slew of Language Changes and Standard Library cuts, rocks the boat with tidal waves of breaking API changes</cite>

An imminent major release continues the pattern: the 2026 devlog reports <cite index="12-3">This is almost entirely a non-breaking change, but there are some observable differences... The follow-up issues to this changeset are the main blockers until we tag Zig 0.17.0</cite> and warns <cite index="12-15,12-16">We'll be releasing 0.17.0 within a couple weeks from now. However, if you don't have time, and you find out that 0.17.0 broke your build, don't worry, there will be plenty of opportunity to get fixes in for the 0.17.1 tag</cite>

Release cadence has historically been inconsistent: <cite index="18-6">the project's release schedule has been a bit inconsistent, with the release of version 0.14 being delayed several times</cite>, corroborated by the maintainer's own slipping estimate: <cite index="31-4,31-6">Previously, I made an estimate of January 1st for the 0.14.0 tag... That deadline slipped by mainly because I was caught up in a rather large branch</cite>

Positive maturity signals: the project does issue dedicated bug-fix-only patch tags rather than folding fixes into the next feature release, e.g. <cite index="28-1,28-2">Bug fixes from 0.14.0 only. Please see the commits or issue tracker to learn which bugs have been fixed.</cite> for the 0.14.1 tag, and all release artifacts are cryptographically signed with a stable minisign key noted across multiple release pages.

Target/platform support is formally tiered and documented rather than ad hoc: <cite index="11-17,11-18">Zig supports a wide range of architectures and operating systems. The Support Table and Additional Platforms sections cover the targets that Zig can build programs for</cite>

Wikipedia's infobox corroborates the current state: <cite index="14-1">Stable release: 0.16 (Beta) / 14 April 2026; 5 months ago</cite> i.e. the 'stable' designation itself is still labeled Beta pre-1.0.

Overall pattern: reproducible, signed, well-documented releases with disciplined patch tagging, but no inter-release compatibility guarantee and routine large-scale breaking changes each cycle, which the rubric's compatibility-guarantee and stability-commitment sub-criteria score low.

selection_and_method_notes.not_used_as_standalone_proxy: GitHub stars/download counts were not used as the sole basis for any subscore.
selection_and_method_notes.predeclared_sampling: Sources selected are the official ziglang.org download/release-notes pages, the official GitHub releases page, official Ubuntu developer documentation, and the top Snap Store listing for 'zig' — all language-neutral, officially-hosted or platform-vendor-hosted pages rather than search-order artifacts. Same retrieval depth (one official channel + one to two OS-vendor channels + one community-tooling check) applied.
